papers.full_text: Abstract Background H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) has been widely spreading among poultry populations for decades. The decline in poultry production performance and the cross-species adaptability it causes will continue to pose threats to the poultry industry and public health. To investigate the prevalence of H9N2 AIV in southeastern China, this study conducted an epidemiological investigation of H9N2 AIV circulating in live poultry markets in Fujian Province, selecting three representative H9N2 virus strains for molecular evolutionary and biological characterization. Results Analysis of the three strains revealed that their HA genes all belonged to the typical B-like lineage, and the NA genes of strains FZ26 and FZ83 originated from the H6N2 subtype, indicating frequent natural reassortment events, and molecular marker analysis revealed mutations at key receptor-binding sites that enhance affinity for human-type receptors. Animal experiments demonstrated that these three H9N2 viruses exhibited certain pathogenicity in chickens but did not cause mortality, suggesting they are low pathogenic viruses. Infected chickens displayed mild clinical symptoms, mainly respiratory-related signs such as head shaking and sneezing. Viral load detection revealed that all three viruses replicated efficiently in the respiratory tissues of chickens, especially in the trachea and lungs. The virus persisted in oropharyngeal and cloacal secretions, with oropharyngeal swabs showing significantly higher viral loads than cloacal swabs, and virus shedding lasted for an extended period. Additionally, histopathological examination found varying degrees of tissue damage in the trachea and lungs of infected chickens. Conclusions In summary, although these three H9N2 virus strains exhibited low pathogenicity, their stable replication ability in the respiratory tract and significant viral shedding characteristics indicate strong transmissibility and potential epidemic risk. These findings highlight the necessity of strengthening virus surveillance and prevention measures in live poultry markets and provide a scientific basis for avian influenza control strategies. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Background H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) has been widely spreading among poultry populations for decades. The decline in poultry production performance and the cross-species adaptability it causes will continue to pose threats to the poultry industry and public health. To investigate the prevalence of H9N2 AIV in southeastern China, this study conducted an epidemiological investigation of H9N2 AIV circulating in live poultry markets in Fujian Province, selecting three representative H9N2 virus strains for molecular evolutionary and biological characterization. Results Analysis of the three strains revealed that their HA genes all belonged to the typical B-like lineage, and the NA genes of strains FZ26 and FZ83 originated from the H6N2 subtype, indicating frequent natural reassortment events, and molecular marker analysis revealed mutations at key receptor-binding sites that enhance affinity for human-type receptors. Animal experiments demonstrated that these three H9N2 viruses exhibited certain pathogenicity in chickens but did not cause mortality, suggesting they are low pathogenic viruses. Infected chickens displayed mild clinical symptoms, mainly respiratory-related signs such as head shaking and sneezing. Viral load detection revealed that all three viruses replicated efficiently in the respiratory tissues of chickens, especially in the trachea and lungs. The virus persisted in oropharyngeal and cloacal secretions, with oropharyngeal swabs showing significantly higher viral loads than cloacal swabs, and virus shedding lasted for an extended period. Additionally, histopathological examination found varying degrees of tissue damage in the trachea and lungs of infected chickens. Conclusions In summary, although these three H9N2 virus strains exhibited low pathogenicity, their stable replication ability in the respiratory tract and significant viral shedding characteristics indicate strong transmissibility and potential epidemic risk. These findings highlight the necessity of strengthening virus surveillance and prevention measures in live poultry markets and provide a scientific basis for avian influenza control strategies. papers.summary_zh: 为研究H9N2禽流感病毒(AIV)在华东地区(患病率)的流行情况,本研究对福建省活禽市场中流行的H9N2 AIV进行了流行病学调查,选取了三种具有代表性的H9N2病毒株进行分子进化和生物学特征分析。结果分析显示,这三种病毒株的HA基因均属于典型的B样系,其中FZ26和FZ83病毒株的NA基因来源于H6N2亚型,表明存在频繁的自然重配事件。分子标记分析显示,在关键受体结合位点存在突变,增强了对人类型受体的亲和力。这些发现强调了在活禽市场中加强病毒监测和预防措施的必要性,并为禽流感防控策略提供了科学依据。伦理声明伦理审批和参与同意动物实验中使用的实验方案已获得福建农林大学动物科学学院研究伦理委员会的批准(许可号:禽流感)。摘要背景H9N2亚型禽流感病毒(AIV)已在禽类群体中广泛传播数十年。其导致的禽类生产性能下降以及跨物种适应性将继续对禽类产业和公共卫生构成威胁。动物实验表明,这三种H9N2病毒在鸡中表现出一定的致病性,但并未引起死亡率,提示它们属于低致病性病毒。感染的鸡表现出轻微的临床症状,主要为与呼吸系统相关的症状,如摇头和打喷嚏。病毒载量检测显示,这三种病毒在鸡的呼吸组织中能够高效复制。

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 为了解我国东南部地区H9N2禽流感病毒的患病率情况,本研究对福建省活禽市场流行的H9N2禽流感病毒进行了流行病学调查,选取了3种具有代表性的H9N2禽流感病毒株进行分子进化和生物学表征。
analysis_zh.methods: 本文中的图像或其他第三方材料已包含在文章的Creative Commons许可中,除非在材料的信用线中另有说明。
analysis_zh.main_results: 动物实验表明,这3种H9N2病毒对鸡表现出一定的致病性,但并未引起死亡率,表明它们是低致病性病毒。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 结论 综上所述,这3种H9N2病毒株虽然致病性较低,但其在呼吸道内稳定的复制能力和显着的病毒排毒特征表明其具有较强的传播性和潜在的流行风险。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些研究结果凸显了加强活禽市场病毒监测和预防措施的必要性,为禽流感的控制策略提供了科学依据。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 中国东南部活禽市场流行的H9N2 禽流感病毒的分子进化和生物学特性。

papers.title: TGF-β3 derived from CD8+ T cells plays an important role in the lungs of piglets infected with SIV
papers.abstract: The swine is considered an important host for the production of pandemic influenza viruses, and studying the immune characteristics of swine influenza virus (SIV) infection in piglets is crucial for pandemic prevention. Here, we used single-cell sequencing (scRNA-seq) to demonstrate that Genotype 4 (G4) reassigned Eurasian avian-like (EA) H1N1 SIV and H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) infection caused significant changes in immune cell composition, gene expression and cell communication. Our study revealed that H1N1 SIV elicits a stronger immune response, and the number of T cells, especially CD8 + T cells, is significantly reduced by infection. Additionally, H1N1 SIV enhanced part of the intercellular communication, especially triggering the T cell-involved transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling pathway network, in which the activation of TGF-β3 ligand receptor signaling is a key regulator. Moreover, flow cytometry and ELISA analysis revealed that H1N1 SIV infection resulted in an increase in TGF-β3 derived from CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, and TGF-β3 is very important to maintain the balance of CD8 + T cell function. The loss of CD8 + T cells can slow weight loss and lung inflammation in the early stage of infection but also affects recovery in the later stage of infection. Overall, these results revealed the presence of TGF-β3, which is rarely mentioned in SIV infection, and elucidated its importance in maintaining the balance of CD8 + T cell function during infection. This study reveals the effects of H1N1 SIV infection on the composition and function of immune cells, and provides new insights into the prevention and treatment of SIV and the prevention of human pandemics.

analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used single-cell sequencing (scRNA-seq) to analyze the effects of Genotype 4 (G4) reassigned Eurasian avian-like (EA) H1N1 SIV and H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) infection on immune cell composition, gene expression, and cell communication in piglets.
analysis.methods: The study employed single-cell sequencing (scRNA-seq) to examine immune cell composition and gene expression changes, and flow cytometry and ELISA analysis were used to measure TGF-β3 levels derived from CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
analysis.main_results: H1N1 SIV infection caused a significant reduction in the number of T cells, particularly CD8+ T cells, and enhanced intercellular communication, especially through the TGF-β3 ligand receptor signaling pathway.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrated that TGF-β3, which is rarely mentioned in SIV infection, plays a critical role in maintaining the balance of CD8+ T cell function during infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide new insights into the immune response to SIV and may inform strategies for the prevention and treatment of SIV and the mitigation of human pandemics.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-only evidence, and the results are based on scRNA-seq and immunological assays, which may not fully capture the in vivo dynamics of immune responses.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the immune characteristics of swine influenza virus (SIV) infection in piglets, highlighting the role of TGF-β3 derived from CD8+ T cells in modulating immune responses. Using single-cell sequencing and immunological assays, the research reveals that H1N1 SIV infection significantly reduces T cell numbers, particularly CD8+ T cells, and enhances intercellular communication through the TGF-β3 signaling pathway. The findings suggest that TGF-β3 is crucial for maintaining CD8+ T cell function during infection, offering new insights into SIV pathogenesis and potential strategies for pandemic prevention. However, the study is based on abstract-only evidence, which may limit the depth of conclusions. The results are relevant for understanding immune dynamics in SIV infections and could inform future research on zoonotic influenza transmission and control.

papers.title: Viral community structure in New Zealand's aquatic birds is associated with scavenging behavior.
papers.abstract: Wild migratory birds play a major role in the global spread of viruses, yet the ecological drivers underpinning viral diversity and transmission, particularly host behavior, remain poorly understood. Aotearoa/New Zealand provides a powerful system to address this, including unique species that reflect its geographical isolation, yet with international connections provided by migratory birds across the East Asian-Australasian Flyway and Antarctic regions. Herein, we conducted a large-scale metatranscriptomic survey of wild birds across New Zealand and its subantarctic islands, in which we collected 1,348 samples from 690 individuals across 31 host species spanning four avian orders. We identified 118 avian viruses from 17 families, including 107 novel species, expanding our knowledge of avian viral diversity. Notably, viral community composition was most strongly associated with bird scavenging behavior, which explained more variation than host taxonomy, geography, or migratory status. Scavenging birds and opportunistic scavengers harbored more diverse viromes than non-scavengers, consistent with increased viral exposure across trophic levels. This was supported by the detection of 12 mammalian-associated viruses, primarily in scavengers, including hedgehog hepatovirus, rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus 2, and sea lion astroviruses, with host sequence data confirming dietary origin. We also detected viruses of epidemiological and evolutionary interest, including a low-pathogenic avian influenza A(H1N9) virus from red knots (Calidris canutus) and a divergent tobanivirus from Auckland Island teal (Anas aucklandica), which represented the first putative avian member of the Tobaniviridae. These findings suggest that virome structure in wild birds is associated with scavenging behavior, thus highlighting the importance of incorporating host ecology into viral surveillance and risk assessment.

papers.title: Influenza A virus neuraminidase-GRP78 binding site prediction.
papers.abstract: Previous research has shown that there is an interaction between Influenza A viral surface neuraminidase (NA) and the host endoplasmic reticulum chaperone GRP78 in the early phases of NA production in the endoplasmic reticulum. In this study, we predict the binding sites of neuraminidase for H1N1, H3N2, and H5N1 strains. We select 13 conserved, cysteine-cyclized regions, one of which is hypothesized to be a possible binding site for GRP78. Using the grand average hydrophobicity index (GRAVY), we focus only on specific highlighted hydrophobic regions, which match the profile of the cyclic peptide, Pep42. Protein-protein docking analysis using HADDOCK suggests that region VIII (C278:C291) is the best possible binding site with the substrate-binding domain β (SBDβ) of GRP78. Subsequently, MDS runs for 150 ns are conducted, and MM-GBSA calculations are done for the three complexes (-7.10, -22.22, and -11.26 kcal/mol for H1N1, H3N2, and H5N1, respectively). The results indicate that GRP78 remains associated with the NA of H3N2, whereas the NAs of H1N1 and H5N1 dissociate from GRP78 during the simulation. Our findings show that region VIII is a potential therapeutic target for neutralizing the viral neuraminidase of seasonal H3N2 flu.
papers.journal: Journal of Biomolecular Structure and Dynamics

papers.title: The evolution of EID pandemics from a planning perspective
papers.abstract: This chapter applies the theoretical concepts outlined in prior chapters to the outbreaks of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in Vietnam during the early 2000s, examining how rapid land use changes influenced disease dynamics. This study explores the specific contributions of peri-urbanization and agricultural consolidation to increased HPAI risk in affected regions. It analyzes how existing planning infrastructure and governance mechanisms responded to the challenge, evaluating their effectiveness in managing an emerging infectious disease threat. This research highlights critical lessons for urban and regional planners, offering insights into developing more resilient systems and effective response strategies for future zoonotic disease outbreaks. These findings underscore the necessity of integrating public health considerations into spatial planning to mitigate the risks associated with evolving human-animal interactions in changing landscapes.

papers.title: Introduction
papers.abstract: This chapter advocates an ecosystem-based approach to preventing global pandemics like COVID-19, emphasizing urban and regional planning’s role in mitigating risks from human-animal interactions and rapid urbanization. It highlights how factors such as agricultural intensification, habitat loss, and global connectivity create disease hotspots, turning local outbreaks into worldwide threats. Drawing on examples like avian influenza, it critiques reactive medical strategies and urges proactive policies, including zoning for safer land use and transportation management. Overall, it positions planners as key to integrating science with policy for a resilient global urban ecosystem, estimating trillions in potential economic savings. By delving into the challenges of unknown risks associated with emerging infectious diseases, adding an ecosystem approach to strictly human health and medical interventions, as well as articulating an associated research agenda, this book details a conceptual framework and associated policy implications designed to bring the skills and expertise of planners to efforts to understand and mitigate future pandemic risks.

papers.source_body_en: This chapter advocates an ecosystem-based approach to preventing global pandemics like COVID-19, emphasizing urban and regional planning’s role in mitigating risks from human-animal interactions and rapid urbanization. It highlights how factors such as agricultural intensification, habitat loss, and global connectivity create disease hotspots, turning local outbreaks into worldwide threats. Drawing on examples like avian influenza, it critiques reactive medical strategies and urges proactive policies, including zoning for safer land use and transportation management. Overall, it positions planners as key to integrating science with policy for a resilient global urban ecosystem, estimating trillions in potential economic savings. By delving into the challenges of unknown risks associated with emerging infectious diseases, adding an ecosystem approach to strictly human health and medical interventions, as well as articulating an associated research agenda, this book details a conceptual framework and associated policy implications designed to bring the skills and expertise of planners to efforts to understand and mitigate future pandemic risks.

news.content: News Rankings Platform Pricing Sign InSign Up Free ← Back to News H5N1 Outbreak Infects Millions of U.S. Poultry By Legis1 Editorial · Edited by Joanne Levine Wednesday, September 9, 2026 · 2 min read Why It Matters Federal agencies and Congress are grappling with an expanding H5N1 outbreak that has infected more than 19,000 wild birds, over 208 million poultry, and 1,168 cattle herds across the U.S. since 2022. A Congressional Research Service (CRS) report titled "Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) in the United States," updated in September, examines the scope of the crisis and the Trump administration's response, laying bare tensions between agricultural stabilization and public health preparedness. Some Members of Congress have expressed concerns about the spread of H5N1 and its potential health effects on humans, as well as its possible negative economic impact on agriculture, especially in the poultry and livestock industries. The Big Picture H5N1 has spread worldwide since a 2021 outbreak in Europe reached the U.S. in early 2022. Migratory pathways can be conduits for the spread of avian influenza to mammals including humans from wild birds. Since March 2024, the virus has infected cattle herds in 20 states, concentrated heavily in California, where 773 of 1,168 confirmed cases occurred. The genotype infecting cattle is believed to have originated from an earlier bird-to-cow transmission event than initially detected. Current strains do not spread readily from person to person. A recent case in Louisiana showed that genetic changes can emerge within an infected patient, suggesting the virus may acquire enhanced ability to infect humans during replication. The USDA announced its Five-Pronged Approach in February 2025, committing $1 billion to the effort, including up to $500 million to biosecurity measures and up to $400 million in aid for flock repopulation. The approach includes reducing regulatory requirements on the chicken and egg industry to stimulate innovation and reduce prices, and exploring pathways toward vaccines, therapeutics, and other strategies for protecting egg-laying poultry. Between January 20, 2025, and July 23, 2026, USDA conducted 4,324 wildlife and domestic biosecurity assessments on U.S. poultry farms. The CDC monitors human cases of H5N1, receives reports from public health laboratories, performs tests in wastewater for the prevalence of H5N1, and provides guidance to state health departments on how to investigate suspected cases. The National Institutes of Health, through its National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, established a research agenda in December 2024 focused on the dairy outbreak and human-transmission potential. Congress has introduced bills addressing surveillance and research. H.R. 766 would authorize the National Wastewater Surveillance System to monitor avian influenza and other zoonotic pathogens. H.R. 2868 in the 119th Congress would designate HPAI study as a high-priority research and extension area under specified U.S. Code provisions for the Secretary of Agriculture. In May 2024, 16 U.S. Senators urged the Secretary of Agriculture to strengthen federal coordination on pathogen surveillance and farmer communication. The Bottom Line The Trump administration's shift toward biosecurity investment and reduced culling represents a departure from traditional stamping-out approaches, though scientists caution that the virus's capacity to adapt and mutate may outpace current surveillance and response capabilities. Federal agencies operating under a One Health framework released in January 2025 face an unresolved tension: whether the current policy mix can contain a pathogen spreading faster than detection systems can track, particularly as H5N1 continues circulating among wild birds, livestock, and domestic poultry. news.content_title: Avian influenza surveillance in poultry environments and pneumonia patients
news.content: Avian influenza viruses are continuing to circulate widely in the environments where humans and poultry intersect in China, even as the country’s aggressive vaccination and culling strategy has suppressed the most dangerous H5 and H7 lineages in recent years. That is the central finding of a new surveillance study published in Virology Journal, in which researchers from the Chinese National Influenza Center and provincial disease control agencies tracked avian influenza viruses across live poultry markets, slaughterhouses, and farms in three Chinese cities over a two-year period, while simultaneously screening hundreds of hospitalized pneumonia patients for signs of zoonotic spillover. The results paint a picture of persistent, low-level viral circulation at the human-animal interface—dominated by the H9 subtype and punctuated by the continued presence of clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses, the same lineage that has swept across continents and caused unprecedented losses in wild birds and poultry worldwide. The study, led by Xiaoxu Zeng, YuWei Weng, Sheng Ye, and Yifei Nie as co-first authors, with Dayan Wang of the Chinese National Influenza Center as corresponding author, was designed as a “multi-section” surveillance effort. Rather than sampling a single type of location or a single population, the team collected environmental specimens from three distinct categories of poultry-exposure settings—live poultry markets where birds are sold and slaughtered on site, commercial slaughterhouses, and poultry farms and backyard flocks—alongside respiratory specimens from patients hospitalized with pneumonia of unknown etiology, or PUE, a surveillance category used to catch severe respiratory infections whose cause is unclear at admission. The fieldwork ran from December 2021 to December 2023, spanning two full years and capturing both autumn-winter peaks and summer troughs of viral activity. The laboratory backbone of the study was real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, or rRT-PCR, a technique that converts viral RNA into DNA and then amplifies and detects it using fluorescent probes. The researchers tested all 8,335 environmental samples for influenza A virus, the broad group that includes all avian influenza subtypes, and then ran subtype-specific assays targeting the H5, H7, H9, and H10 hemagglutinin subtypes. The hemagglutinin protein, the “H” in subtype names such as H5N1 or H9N2, is the viral surface molecule that determines which receptors the virus can bind and, largely, which species it can infect. Among human respiratory specimens, the team screened 840 samples from hospitalized PUE patients. The headline number from the environmental sampling is striking: 32.2 percent of the 8,335 samples tested positive for influenza A virus. In other words, nearly one in three swabs taken from places where people routinely come into contact with poultry, poultry products, or poultry waste carried detectable avian influenza genetic material. The subtype breakdown was dominated by H9, which was detected in 20.1 percent of all samples—a reminder that this low-pathogenic subtype, which causes mild or asymptomatic disease in birds, is endemic in Chinese poultry production systems. H5, the subtype that includes both highly pathogenic and low-pathogenic variants, accounted for 7.1 percent of samples. H10 appeared only sporadically at 0.2 percent, and H7—the subtype behind severe human H7N9 outbreaks in China between 2013 and 2017—was not detected at all, a result consistent with the effectiveness of China’s poultry vaccination campaigns against that lineage. Seasonality emerged as a clear pattern. Positive rates for both H5 and H9 were higher during autumn and winter months, mirroring the well-documented winter seasonality of respiratory influenza viruses and possibly reflecting cooler temperatures that prolong viral survival in the environment, along with increased poultry production and trade around winter holidays. Comparing the two study years, the median monthly positive rates for H5 and H9 were lower in 2023 than in 2022, although the researchers note that this downward trend did not reach statistical significance—a distinction that matters, because a non-significant decline could reflect sampling variability rather than a true reduction in viral circulation. Geography within the poultry supply chain also mattered. H5 and H9 positive rates were generally higher in live poultry markets and slaughterhouses than in farms and backyard flocks. This gradient makes biological and operational sense: markets and slaughterhouses concentrate birds from many sources, creating opportunities for viral amplification and environmental contamination, while farms represent the upstream end of the chain where birds have had fewer opportunities for cross-contamination. The finding reinforces a recurring theme in influenza surveillance—live poultry markets are the critical bottleneck where avian viruses accumulate and where human exposure risk is highest. The researchers went beyond simple positive rates by comparing specific environmental sample categories within these settings—cutting boards, drinking water, blood sewage, and other surfaces and fluids commonly sampled in poultry environments. Here the results diverged by subtype. H5 showed no statistically significant difference across sample categories (P = 0.06), but H9 did (P = 0.03), with significantly higher median positive rates found on cutting boards and in blood sewage than in drinking water. This detail has practical implications: cutting boards, where raw poultry is chopped at markets and in food preparation, and blood sewage, the contaminated liquid waste generated during slaughter, represent the environmental niches where H9 viruses persist most reliably. The finding suggests that hygiene interventions targeting these specific fomites and waste streams—disinfection of cutting surfaces, proper treatment of slaughter waste—could disproportionately reduce environmental viral load. To understand the genetic identity and evolutionary relationships of the circulating viruses, the team sequenced the hemagglutinin genes of H5, H9, and H10 viruses detected in the environment and performed phylogenetic analysis, the computational reconstruction of evolutionary family trees from genetic sequence data. All of the viruses belonged to the Eurasian lineage, one of the two great evolutionary branches of avian influenza (the other being the North American lineage), reflecting the movement of viruses among birds across Eurasia. Critically, the H5 viruses clustered in clade 2.3.4.4b, the globally dominant H5 clade responsible for the ongoing panzootic that has devastated wild bird populations and spread to mammalian species on multiple continents. Its continued detection in Chinese poultry environments confirms that this lineage remains entrenched at the human-animal interface in the region, despite vaccination efforts. Perhaps the most sobering finding came from the phylogenetic comparison between environmental and human viruses. Several H9 viruses recovered from environmental samples were found to be closely related to representative human H9N2 viruses—meaning the viruses circulating in market environments were genetically near neighbors of viruses known to have infected people. H9N2 is considered one of the most important zoonotic influenza lineages because it possesses receptor-binding and other genetic features compatible with human infection, and it serves as an internal gene donor in reassortment events, the process by which co-infecting influenza viruses exchange genome segments to generate novel combinations. Human infections with H9N2 are typically mild and often go undetected, which means the true spillover burden is likely underestimated—a concern amplified by the genetic proximity documented in this study. Against this backdrop of persistent environmental contamination, the human surveillance results were, in a sense, reassuring. Of the 840 respiratory specimens from hospitalized patients with pneumonia of unknown etiology, 86 tested positive for seasonal influenza viruses—the ordinary human influenza A and B strains that cause annual epidemics. However, none of the 840 specimens tested positive for H5, H7, H9, or H10. No zoonotic spillover events were captured among severe pneumonia cases during the study period, suggesting that whatever low-level human infections with these subtypes may be occurring, they did not translate into hospitalizations with severe pneumonia in these three cities during the surveillance window. The authors emphasize that their findings should be read as a call for continued vigilance rather than comfort. Multiple avian influenza subtypes continued to circulate in poultry-exposure environments throughout the study, with H5 clade 2.3.4.4b—an H5 lineage with demonstrated pandemic potential—still present, and H9 viruses genetically linked to known human infections persisting at high rates in the very settings where human exposure is most intense. The research team advocates for sustained, multi-site “One Health” surveillance—an integrated approach that monitors human, animal, and environmental health as a connected system—covering both poultry-exposure environments and human populations. Such surveillance, they argue, is essential to track the ongoing evolution and reassortment of avian influenza viruses and to detect zoonotic spillover events early, before they have the chance to seed larger outbreaks. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, with informed consent obtained from all participants, and was funded in part by China’s National Science and Technology Major Project for the Prevention and Control of Emerging and Major Infectious Diseases, along with China CDC–US CDC collaboration programs and provincial health research grants. As avian influenza viruses continue their global expansion—driven by clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses spreading through migratory birds and poultry trade—the study offers both a methodological template and a warning: the environment where humans and poultry meet remains heavily seeded with influenza viruses, and only continuous monitoring at that interface can reveal whether the next subtype to jump the species barrier is already quietly gathering the genetic tools to do so. This detail has practical implications: cutting boards, where raw poultry is chopped at markets and in food preparation, and blood sewage, the contaminated liquid waste generated during slaughter, represent the environmental niches where H9 viruses persist most reliably. The finding suggests that hygiene interventions targeting these specific fomites and waste streams—disinfection of cutting surfaces, proper treatment of slaughter waste—could disproportionately reduce environmental viral load. To understand the genetic identity and evolutionary relationships of the circulating viruses, the team sequenced the hemagglutinin genes of H5, H9, and H10 viruses detected in the environment and performed phylogenetic analysis, the computational reconstruction of evolutionary family trees from genetic sequence data. All of the viruses belonged to the Eurasian lineage, one of the two great evolutionary branches of avian influenza (the other being the North American lineage), reflecting the movement of viruses among birds across Eurasia. Critically, the H5 viruses clustered in clade 2.3.4.4b, the globally dominant H5 clade responsible for the ongoing panzootic that has devastated wild bird populations and spread to mammalian species on multiple continents. Its continued detection in Chinese poultry environments confirms that this lineage remains entrenched at the human-animal interface in the region, despite vaccination efforts. Perhaps the most sobering finding came from the phylogenetic comparison between environmental and human viruses. Several H9 viruses recovered from environmental samples were found to be closely related to representative human H9N2 viruses—meaning the viruses circulating in market environments were genetically near neighbors of viruses known to have infected people. H9N2 is considered one of the most important zoonotic influenza lineages because it possesses receptor-binding and other genetic features compatible with human infection, and it serves as an internal gene donor in reassortment events, the process by which co-infecting influenza viruses exchange genome segments to generate novel combinations. Human infections with H9N2 are typically mild and often go undetected, which means the true spillover burden is likely underestimated—a concern amplified by the genetic proximity documented in this study. Against this backdrop of persistent environmental contamination, the human surveillance results were, in a sense, reassuring. Of the 840 respiratory specimens from hospitalized patients with pneumonia of unknown etiology, 86 tested positive for seasonal influenza viruses—the ordinary human influenza A and B strains that cause annual epidemics. However, none of the 840 specimens tested positive for H5, H7, H9, or H10. No zoonotic spillover events were captured among severe pneumonia cases during the study period, suggesting that whatever low-level human infections with these subtypes may be occurring, they did not translate into hospitalizations with severe pneumonia in these three cities during the surveillance window. The authors emphasize that their findings should be read as a call for continued vigilance rather than comfort. Multiple avian influenza subtypes continued to circulate in poultry-exposure environments throughout the study, with H5 clade 2.3.4.4b—an H5 lineage with demonstrated pandemic potential—still present, and H9 viruses genetically linked to known human infections persisting at high rates in the very settings where human exposure is most intense. The research team advocates for sustained, multi-site “One Health” surveillance—an integrated approach that monitors human, animal, and environmental health as a connected system—covering both poultry-exposure environments and human populations. Such surveillance, they argue, is essential to track the ongoing evolution and reassortment of avian influenza viruses and to detect zoonotic spillover events early, before they have the chance to seed larger outbreaks. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, with informed consent obtained from all participants, and was funded in part by China’s National Science and Technology Major Project for the Prevention and Control of Emerging and Major Infectious Diseases, along with China CDC–US CDC collaboration programs and provincial health research grants. As avian influenza viruses continue their global expansion—driven by clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses spreading through migratory birds and poultry trade—the study offers both a methodological template and a warning: the environment where humans and poultry meet remains heavily seeded with influenza viruses, and only continuous monitoring at that interface can reveal whether the next subtype to jump the species barrier is already quietly gathering the genetic tools to do so. news.content_zh: 在人类与家禽接触的环境中,禽流感病毒仍在广泛传播,尽管中国近年来采取了积极的疫苗接种和扑杀策略,成功抑制了最危险的H5和H7谱系。这是发表在《病毒学杂志》上的一项新监测研究的核心发现。研究人员来自中国国家流感中心和省级疾病预防控制机构,他们在三个中国城市对活禽市场、屠宰场和农场进行了为期两年的追踪,同时对数百名住院肺炎患者进行筛查,以寻找人兽共患跨物种溢出的迹象。研究结果描绘了在人类与动物接触界面持续存在的低水平病毒传播现象——主要由H9亚型主导,并且偶尔出现2.3.4.4b分支H5病毒,这一谱系曾席卷全球,导致野生鸟类和家禽在全球范围内造成前所未有的损失。该研究由曾小旭、翁宇薇、叶胜和聂毅斐作为共同第一作者,王大年(中国国家流感中心)作为通讯作者领导,其设计为。

analysis.brief_en: CIDRAP reported on Sep 10, 2026, that turkey farms in Dakotas and Minnesota are affected by H5N1 avian flu. The report highlights the outbreak but does not specify the number of cases, deaths, or exposures. It also does not detail the response measures taken by authorities. The information is part of CIDRAP's broader coverage of public health issues, including vaccine-related topics and zoonotic diseases. The H5N1 avian flu is a primary candidate for analysis under the avian influenza profile, and the report does not mention any related entities like seasonal influenza or swine influenza. The outbreak is under investigation, and no specific risk level is stated in the evidence.

news.content: Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine SEP 09, 2026 Bird Flu Cases Are on the Rise WRITTEN BY: Savannah Logan A strain of bird flu, H5N1, is spreading in Australia and around the world, and backyard bird feeders may be making the problem worse. The H5N1 strain of the virus was identified in 2020 and has infected both birds and mammals across the globe. This strain, which evolved new variants in 2021, is deadlier than previous strains and has caused neurological disease and death in multiple species of both birds and mammals. Human infections with H5N1 have been rare, and no human-human transmission has been documented. However, bird populations in multiple countries have been decimated, and more populations are at risk from this strain. Now, studies suggest that backyard birdfeeders may create transmission hotspots for wild birds. Backyard birdfeeders create a unique environment for spreading disease because they bring together different bird species and large numbers of birds that would not normally congregate in nature. This close contact can lead to super spreader events in wild bird populations. These birds can then spread H5N1 to scavengers that may eat the carcasses of the infected birds, and it can even lead to human infections in people who regularly interact with animals, such as wildlife biologists and veterinarians. To minimize transmission and the risk of contracting bird flu, the best practice is to avoid feeding wild birds via birdfeeders. Additionally, hand feeding is not recommended since it can bring potentially infected birds in close contact and increase the risk of human transmission. While the current strain does not appear to spread between humans once contracted, mutations are always possible that could lead to greater risk. Minimizing both bird-bird and bird-human contact is the best practice for stopping the spread of this strain of bird flu, which will help preserve wild bird populations and minimize risk to humans. Sources: The Conversation, The Conversation, Science Daily Related Content Takeout Contains More Salt than Advertised Intermittent Fasting Keeps Weight Off for a Year How PFAS Regulations Are Driving Chromatography Procurement Across Federal Agencies

news.content: Skip to main contentEnable accessibility for low visionOpen the accessibility menu News FactCheck Photos Press Releases About Support Us Menu Factual. Independent. Impartial. News Newsroom FactCheck Photos Press Releases About Support Us Contact Us FAQ Legal and Privacy Terms Of Use Follow us Facebook Apple News Instagram AAP FactCheck Latest FactChecks Resources How We Work Who We Are Contact Submit A Claim Share Facebook X (Twitter) Copy Link Download Follow Facebook Apple News Instagram Share Facebook x Copy Link Download Bird flu denial sweeps social media as Australian cases surge Christine Lee September 08, 2026 Australian wildlife has already been impacted by bird flu, despite false claims online. Image by Darren England/AAP PHOTOS WHAT WAS CLAIMED No cases of bird flu have been detected in Australia. OUR VERDICT False. Hundreds of H5 bird flu cases have been confirmed in Australian wildlife. AAP FactCheck - The rollout of bird flu vaccinations in Australia is fuelling misinformation online, including false claims that no cases of the disease have been detected in the country. In fact, the government has confirmed hundreds of H5 bird flu infections in wildlife since the first Australian case was detected in June 2026. The claim was made in an August 19 Facebook video1 by an Australian user who questions the purpose of bird flu vaccination programs. "So just a reminder, there's been no detections of this bird flu," the user says in the post (timestamp four minutes 42 seconds). The Facebook user also suggests birds did not have a "problem" with the flu before the development of bird flu vaccines. "So we now look in mid-last year where they're starting to develop and test these vaccines on king penguins that have, you know, birds have been around for millions of years, never had a problem with the flu or anything," the user says (timestamp 3:05). Avian flu has been detected in a range of Australian wildlife, including some mammals. (Susie Dodds/AAP PHOTOS2) The claim that Australia has not detected any cases of bird flu is baseless. Australia's first confirmed detections of the disease were announced in a June 20 federal government media release3 and occurred in two migratory seabirds - a brown skua and a giant petrel. Both birds were found in an isolated area near Esperance, Western Australia, according to the media release. The first case of bird flu in a Phillip Island little penguin was reported by ABC News4 on August 15 - four days before the Facebook video was posted. The Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) data dashboard5 lists 484 confirmed H5 bird flu events in Australian wildlife as of September 4. The list includes several mammal species found with H5 bird flu infections, including red foxes, long-nosed fur seals and a bottlenose dolphin. PCR tests are the primary frontline method for diagnosing avian flu, according to CSIRO6, Australia's national science agency. Scientists from CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness also conduct sequencing tests that provide the virus's specific genetic sequence. "This can be compared to reference samples from other confirmed cases to give details such as the strain of the virus, where the virus is likely to be from and how it has or hasn't changed," a CSIRO spokesperson told AAP FactCheck. The first known case of avian flu dates to an outbreak in poultry in Italy in 1878. (EPA PHOTO7) In the video, the Australian Facebook user also questions the reliability of PCR tests for detecting bird flu (timestamp 4:46). However, AAP FactCheck previously debunked8 similar false claims that PCR tests have no diagnostic capability to detect the virus, with experts saying they are highly accurate when used correctly. The claim that birds have not historically been "troubled" by flu is also false. Michael Ward9, an infectious disease expert at the University of Sydney's school of veterinary science, said avian influenza had been documented for more than a century. "Avian influenza has been reported and studied since at least the late 1800s, when it was called 'fowl plague'," Professor Ward told AAP FactCheck. Prof Ward said the first description of avian influenza dated back to an outbreak of disease10 in poultry in northern Italy in 1878. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) website11 similarly traces the first recorded case of avian influenza to northern Italy in 1878. Deadly H5N1 Avian Flu Mutation Poses Serious Threat to Australia’s Wildlife Techno 07.09.2026 - 21:08 222 viewed Journalist Anna Tkach Небезпечна мутація пташиного грипу H5N1 загрожує життю диких тварин в Австралії. Photo: НВ — Техно The Rising Danger of H5N1 Avian Influenza to Wild Animals On September 7, 2023, researchers from Deakin University's Centre for Marine Science revealed alarming findings about the H5N1 avian influenza virus threatening Australia's natural fauna. Previously considered low risk, the virus has undergone mutations resulting in a highly lethal strain. This evolution is causing devastating impacts on various bird species and marine mammals, as pathogenic H5N1 variants continue to wreak havoc on wildlife populations globally. Species Most at Risk Colonial seabirds are particularly vulnerable to this mutated virus, including: Australian terns waterfowl ducks birds of prey crows magpies In Australia, large-scale die-offs of large terns have been recorded, indicating the virus's transmission from oceanic storm-petrels to coastal wildlife. Similar outbreaks have been reported elsewhere, such as mass mortality among sea lions in South America. In Australia, the virus’s spread has also extended to seals and dolphins. Volunteers play a crucial role in monitoring animal deaths. The public is urged to avoid contact with sick or deceased wildlife and to immediately report sightings to a 24/7 emergency hotline staffed by specialists equipped with protective gear. As Sarah Riding explains, “It’s easier to identify which birds are unlikely to be affected by the H5N1 strain. However, specific behavioral traits significantly increase the infection risks for certain species.” This outbreak highlights the critical need for ongoing wildlife surveillance and protection efforts. The persistence of H5N1 poses serious threats not only to biodiversity but also to economic sectors, as the health of wild animals directly influences agriculture and ecosystem stability. Prompt intervention and adherence to safety protocols are essential to halt further virus spread and safeguard vulnerable species. The emergence of this deadly H5N1 strain raises critical questions about the potential pathways for its spread across Australia. Understanding these transmission routes is essential for developing effective response strategies. For a deeper insight into how avian influenza could proliferate in the region, you can explore four possible scenarios for avian influenza spread in Australia. Here’s what you can do Published: September 9, 2026 4:08pm EDT As a veterinarian who studies infectious diseases in cats, I’ve been repeatedly asked whether Australia’s outbreak of the H5 bird flu poses a risk to pets. The short answer is yes. As this lethal virus continues to infect more mammals, poultry farmers and backyard chook owners remain on high alert. But outbreaks overseas suggest pets – particularly cats – can also contract H5 bird flu and develop severe disease. To date, Australia has not recorded any cases of the deadly H5 bird flu in pets and the risk to most cats and dogs remains very low. But if infection does happen, the consequences can be serious. As a nation of pet owners – with 7.7 million Australian households sharing their homes with a pet – we must understand how cats and dogs may become infected, what signs to watch for and which practical measures can reduce exposure to H5 bird flu. Not just birds Cats and dogs can catch bird flu in four main ways: direct contact with infected wildlife being in places where infected wildlife have been eating or drinking infected animal products coming into contact with the virus at home, including via clothing, shoes or equipment. H5 bird flu outbreaks abroad – including in Poland, South Korea and Belgium – suggest infected cats can deteriorate rapidly and often die within days of exposure. Dogs can also become infected but appear less vulnerable to severe sickness. Many develop only mild symptoms or none at all. Currently, no vaccinations are available for pets, and there is limited data on whether existing influenza antivirals could be a safe and effective treatment for cats and dogs. This means prevention is the most effective tool we have. Read more: The first wave of bird flu is the worst: what Australia can learn from overseas How would I know if my pet is infected? The early signs of H5 bird flu infection resemble those of many common animal diseases. Infected pets may initially look unwell, develop a fever, become lethargic and go off their food. Common respiratory signs include coughing, difficulty breathing and discharge from the eyes or nose. In cats, H5 bird flu can quickly progress and lead to serious neurological symptoms such as tremors, seizures or sudden blindness. If your pet develops any of these symptoms, don’t arrive at your veterinary clinic unannounced. Call ahead and discuss your concerns with a vet, telling them if your pet has recently had contact with wild birds, wildlife or raw animal products. This will allow your vet to assess your pet’s level of risk and determine the safest way to examine them. If your vet suspects your pet may have bird flu, they may conduct an initial assessment outside the hospital and implement additional infection control measures, such as wearing protective clothing and caring for your pet separately from other animals. They may also consult with the government veterinarian coordinating the bird flu response in your area. If directed to do so by the government veterinarian, your vet may collect samples – most commonly respiratory swabs similar to COVID tests – to determine whether H5 bird flu could be involved. Currently, there is no in-house test that veterinary clinics can perform, so samples must be sent to a dedicated government laboratory for analysis. Read more: What happens next with bird flu? An expert explains why monitoring matters What you can do Here are four practical steps owners can take to help keep their pets safe. 1. Avoid contact with wildlife Leashing dogs and keeping cats indoors where possible will stop them from touching, scavenging or hunting infected wildlife. This also prevents pets from hunting healthy native wildlife, which need all the help they can get as this virus spreads. 2. Stay away from contaminated environments H5 bird flu can be present in bird droppings, feathers, carcasses and contaminated water. Depending on environmental conditions, the virus can survive for days or even weeks. To protect your pet, bring food and water bowls inside when not in use and cover outdoor cat enclosures with roofing or tarp to keep contaminated bird droppings out. You can also shift bird baths and feeders from areas your pet frequents or remove them altogether. Read more: Backyard bird feeding could be a bird flu ‘superspreader’. An expert explains 3. Steer clear of raw animal products H5 bird flu is likely to spread into poultry or other farmed animals, making raw animal products a potential source of infection. Most feline cases overseas occurred when cats ate raw foods – including raw meat, unpasteurised dairy products and improperly processed pet food – later found to be contaminated with the virus. Owners should avoid feeding their pets such products. And it’s worth noting, freezing or freeze-drying food does not reliably kill or inactivate avian influenza viruses. 4. Don’t bring the virus home To avoid accidentally infecting your pet, it’s important to boost hygiene measures. This is especially true if you work with birds, wildlife or farmed poultry. Only handle sick or injured wildlife if you are trained to do so. If you do have contact with them, wash your hands thoroughly, disinfect any equipment and change clothing and footwear before returning home. For most Australian pets, the risk of getting H5 bird flu is extremely low. Taking some simple precautions can help keep it that way. If you encounter sick or dead wildlife, remember to “avoid, record and report” any sightings to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. You can stay informed about where H5 bird flu has been detected by regularly checking the Australian government’s bird flu website and detection map. Read more: Australia has long relied on volunteers and wildlife carers. news.content_title: Bird flu threatens French foie gras amid new duck cull
news.content: More than 7,600 Mulard ducks have been culled after an outbreak of H5N1 bird flu was detected on a farm in western France. The latest outbreak is another blow to France's foie gras industry, which saw prices spike in 2023 after 35 million forced-fed fowl were culled in the 2022-2023 season after a similar outbreak. The industry also faces mounting pressure from animal rights activists over claims of animal cruelty. At least 15 French towns and cities – including Bordeaux, Lyon, Montpellier, and Pessac – have banned foie gras from being served at official government receptions and publicly funded events over animal welfare concerns. The H5N1 outbreak is the first to be declared in France in several months and is unusually early for the bird flu season, which usually picks up around late October. Many French cities are banning foie gras at public events - JULIEN DE ROSA/AFP The movement of poultry and other captive birds within a 10km radius of the affected farm, which is located in Maine-et-Loire, has now been prohibited to try to stop the outbreak from going any further, according to the French agricultural agency. The aim of the cull was to "limit the risk of the virus spreading to other farms," said the local authority. Within the 10km restriction zone, "the movement of poultry and other captive birds is prohibited". Though traditionally made with Geese, ducks now account for 98 per cent of the foie gras produced in France. The birds are much cheaper to raise and easier to handle, although connoisseurs say goose-based foie gras has a more "subtle and delicate" flavour. The latest cull - like previous ones - was undertaken to protect both animal and human health. Ducks are killed to stop the spread of the disease between farms, as well as to protect the health of farmers and minimise the risk of the virus mutating. It is thought foie gras itself does not pose a risk to human health, even if it came from a bird-flu-infected duck, because it is almost always heat-treated before it is sold, which effectively destroys the virus, according to Public Health France. "The consumption of meat, foie gras and eggs – and more generally of any food product based on poultry – presents no risk to humans," said a spokesman for the Maine-et-Loire prefecture. Veterinary experts say ducks are especially problematic regarding H5N1 because they can carry the virus without showing symptoms and have been described as the Chevaux de Troie or "Trojan horses" of bird flu. It is unclear how the birds in the latest outbreak, located on a farm in Longué-Jumelles, contracted the virus, although it is typically spread by wild birds which shed the virus through their droppings. It is for this reason that British poultry were f orced into lockdown or "flockdown" from late October to April of this year. This included so-called "free-range" birds, which, as the Telegraph reported in November continued to be described as free-range despite never seeing the light of day under a dispensation given by the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs (DEFRA). Ducks reared for foie gras typically spend the first 90 days of their lives being reared in their tens of thousands in barns with very little access to natural light. Animal rights campaigners say most never see water. They then are put through a rigorous 12-16 day "fattening up" period where they are force-fed through a tube to significantly enlarge their livers, before being slaughtered. While France introduced a vaccination programme to protect its duck population from bird flu in 2023, the jabs do not entirely stop the virus from getting into a flock. Data collected by the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health & Safety suggested that between 50 and 55 per cent of the country's ducks are unvaccinated at any given time, due to a 20-day gap between the first and second dose of the vaccine and waning immunity over time. The ducks subject to the latest bird-flu cull in Western France had received their first dose of the H5N1 vaccine, but not the second, meaning they were not fully protected, according to the disease monitoring firm Airfinity. The threat to France's £2 billion foie gras industry comes amid increasing global competition. Once the dominant producer, it is now being challenged by China, which has rapidly scaled up its output of the delicacy and now accounts for 45 per cent of global production. A tin of Chinese foie gras costs roughly £3.70, while a typical tin of French foie gras made from duck liver costs between £10 and £15. French foie gras produced from Geese costs anywhere between £70 and £150. China is also said to operate a more rigorous poultry vaccination programme, according to an analysis by DEFRA. It applies to all farmed birds in the country, which has managed to keep outbreaks of bird flu on farms relatively low compared with European levels. The H5N1 avian flu pandemic has now been running for six years and has decimated flocks of farmed chickens and turkeys across the globe. In the UK alone, more than five million farmed birds have been culled since 2021, costing an estimated £48 million in farmers' compensation alone. Last week, the virus was detected on a mink farm in the US state of Utah . Minks in captivity have previously been described as pandemic "time bombs". The size and density of fur farms – where thousands of the animals are crammed together in tight proximity – give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate. The virus has also done huge damage to wild birds and other animals. In South America alone, more than 600,000 wild seabirds have died since 2022. Dozens of other mammals have been infected and died across the globe, including foxes, otters, sea lions, bears, and seals. In June, the virus was found in Australia for the first time – the last continent on earth to record a case – and the government has since launched a vaccination programme to protect the country's rare species, including birds like orange-bellied parrots and black cockatoos. Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 gains the mutations necessary to spread between people, it could trigger a human-pandemic, something that would be of "enormous concern", according to the World Health Organization (WHO), given the virus's 50 per cent case fatality rate. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Turkey farms in Dakotas, Minnesota hit with H5N1 avian flu News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share Copied to clipboard Mizzou CAFNR, Morgan Lieberman / Flickr cc Since September 1, the US Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) has noted seven H5N1 avian flu detections in commercial poultry operations, in North and South Dakota, Minnesota, and Idaho. In Wright County, Minnesota, 29,800 birds at a turkey facility were affected, as were 61,300 birds at a commercial turkey operation in McPherson County, South Dakota, and 43,800 turkeys at a facility in Turner County, South Dakota. In Lamoure County, North Dakota, 41,600 commercial birds were hit. In addition, H5N1 was confirmed in a commercial poultry breeding operation in Edmunds County, South Dakota, housing 30,200 birds, and Idaho confirmed two backyard outbreaks in Canyon and Gem counties. Overall in the past 30 days eight commercial flocks and six backyard flocks have been infected by avian flu, affecting 360,000 birds. Cattle in Idaho also infected In other avian flu news, there are two new infected dairy herds in cattle in Idaho. In the past 30 days, Idaho and Texas have reported H5N1 in five dairy herds. So far this year there have been 88 H5N1 detections in cattle. WHO approves multi-dose maternal RSV vaccine to protect more infants News brief Liz Szabo, MA Topics Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Prostock Studio / iStock The World Health Organization (WHO) has prequalified a version of the maternal vaccine against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) that includes several doses in one vial. Vaccinating pregnant people in the third trimester protects their newborns against RSV infection and reduces a baby’s risk of being hospitalized with the virus by more than 80%. Vaccines need the WHO’s seal of approval before United Nations agencies such as UNICEF can buy them to distribute to lower-income countries. Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, agreed last year to fund the introduction of maternal RSV vaccination in multiple countries, and has been working to lay the groundwork for its rollout. Although the WHO prequalified single-dose vials in 2025, Gavi’s maternal RSV vaccination program could not begin until the agency prequalified multi-dose vials, which reduce the cost and difficulty of mass immunizations. Benefits of multi-dose vials Multi-dose vials allow healthcare professionals to vaccinate more people, but take up less storage space on delivery trucks or in clinics. Multi-dose products also make it easier to maintain a “cold chain,” in which vaccines are refrigerated at an appropriate temperature on the journey from the factory into people’s arms. RSV hospitalizes 3.6 million and kills 100,000 children under age five years each year, according to the WHO. Newborns are especially vulnerable. Pfizer released the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, in the United States in 2023. The Gates Foundation provided funding to develop a multi-dose version. Getting the multi-dose product prequalified “is a key milestone for RSV and, more broadly, for pneumonia prevention and reducing infant mortality globally,” said Ignacio Esteban, Gavi’s senior policy manager and incoming head of the adult and adolescent vaccines portfolio. CDC warns of new Salmonella outbreak linked to broccoli sprouts News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Foodborne Disease Salmonella Cyclospora Jovan J / Flickr cc The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) yesterday announced a new Salmonella outbreak linked to broccoli sprouts produced by Evergreen Fresh Sprouts. So far at least 22 people in four states have been sickened, and two patients have been hospitalized. No deaths have been linked to this outbreak. The sprouts were sold to food co-ops, restaurants, food service customers, and grocery stores in Idaho, Montana, and Washington. Sixteen people in Washington state have been sickened, four in Montana, and one each in Idaho and Utah. Illnesses started on dates ranging from July 7 to August 26. The sprouts were packaged in plastics bags or clam shell containers with expiration dates of 9/7, 9/9, 9/11, 9/14, and 9/16. The CDC said consumers should toss any sprouts meeting that description. CDC adds 1,150 more Cyclospora cases to US total In other food outbreak news, yesterday the CDC added 1,150 Cyclospora cases to the US total, lifting the caseload to 19,595 infections. The agency said it is investigating 9,355 additional lab-confirmed cases and 6,149 suspected cases. “Recent illnesses may not yet be reported due to the time it takes to identify and report Cyclospora cases,” the CDC said. "It takes about six weeks from the start of symptoms to when CDC receives the case information.” In case you missed it Previous Next Study: Candida auris often spreads from patients to gloves, gowns of healthcare workers Ebola outbreak in DR Congo tops 6,600 cases Lawmakers criticize deal that would send NIH funds to Department of Defense Mom’s Tdap vaccination doesn’t affect baby’s growth, analysis finds Quick takes: Dengue rise in Florida, South Dakota anthrax detection, drop in foreign food inspections Bacteria in classroom dust may contribute to slightly lower lung function in kids Quick takes: Cyclosporiasis in Michigan, Aedes mosquitoes in the UK, new NYC Legionnaires measures Regular exercise before COVID infection linked to better daily function 2 years later This week's top reads COVID-19 may trigger the same immune pathway as lupus A new study sheds light on the immune cells responsible for producing autoantibodies in people with COVID. Some studies suggest that flu, shingles, and tuberculosis vaccines could protect against neurologic diseases such as Alzheimer’s. analysis.time: Since September 1, 2026, and ongoing. The outbreak has been reported as of the publication date on 2026-09-10.
analysis.location_and_population: Commercial poultry operations in North and South Dakota, Minnesota, and Idaho, affecting a total of 360,000 birds. Cattle in Idaho were also infected.
analysis.event: H5N1 avian flu was detected in commercial poultry operations in the mentioned states, with specific facilities in Wright County, Minnesota; McPherson County, South Dakota; Turner County, South Dakota; and Lamoure County, North Dakota affected. Additionally, H5N1 was confirmed in a commercial poultry breeding operation in Edmunds County, South Dakota, and two backyard outbreaks in Idaho.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: A total of 360,000 birds were affected in the past 30 days, including eight commercial flocks and six backyard flocks. No deaths have been linked to the avian flu outbreak, but the risk of spread and impact on the poultry industry is significant.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The US Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) has noted the detections. The CDC is investigating additional cases and advising consumers to discard affected broccoli sprouts. The situation remains under active monitoring and investigation.

analysis.brief_en: In September 2026, H5N1 avian flu outbreaks were reported in commercial poultry operations across North and South Dakota, Minnesota, and Idaho. The US Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) documented seven detections in the past 30 days, with specific facilities in Wright County, Minnesota; McPherson County, South Dakota; Turner County, South Dakota; and Lamoure County, North Dakota affected. A commercial poultry breeding operation in Edmunds County, South Dakota, also confirmed H5N1, along with two backyard outbreaks in Idaho. The total number of birds impacted reached 360,000, including eight commercial flocks and six backyard flocks. While no deaths have been linked to the outbreak, the risk of spread and impact on the poultry industry is significant. The CDC is investigating the situation and has advised consumers to discard broccoli sprouts associated with the outbreak. The response remains ongoing with active monitoring and investigation.

Forgotten Password Cancel Home / Featured Content / Thousands of Little Penguins Will Be Vaccinated Against Bird Flu Down Under Thousands of Little Penguins Will Be Vaccinated Against Bird Flu Down Under H5N1 virus spreading quickly in Australia with coastal birds and other wildlife threatened September 9, 2026 by Global Voices Leave a Comment By Kevin Rennie The arrival of H5N1 bird flu in Australia presents serious challenges, especially for wildlife. While bird flu has been plaguing the rest of the world for years, Australia had been free of the virus until a case was identified on June 20. News that numerous wild birds had died from the virus prompted authorities to launch a vaccination campaign, with Victoria’s little penguin colonies at St Kilda and Phillip Island top of the list. Julie Old, Associate Professor in Biology, Zoology and Animal Science, Western Sydney University, explained the vaccination process in an article with The Conversation: Capturing wildlife to vaccinate them is difficult, particularly because the bird flu vaccination requires they be caught twice, for two doses. However, little penguins are flightless, live in colonies and return at night to the same burrow, making them easier to capture and vaccinate. Most Victorians seemed pleased by the announcement. However, it was not long before anti-vaccination voices appeared on social media. Josh Burns, whose House of Representatives seat of McNamara covers the St Kilda penguins, posted on Instagram: Video Player is loading. Predictably, many of those were trolling the politician with anti-vaccination sentiments. These comments were typical of their responses: One user shared: Well that’ll be the end of those little penguins then Another said: When the human population wake up. They just move on to wildlife to keep the money flowing. This negativity was no surprise to Mark Andrew: ohhh my god, the cookers will be out in force Cookerpedia was an Aussie site active during the COVID-19 pandemic. It documented “the activities of individuals in Australia who are cookers.” Cooker is an Australian slang word for people who believe a wide range of conspiracy theories, whether mainstream or fringe. Mark Gwynn of the Australian National Dictionary Center shared how the term became an Australianism in an email interview with Global Voices: We’ve drafted up an entry for the Australian National Dictionary, so at this stage we consider this sense to have originated here and to only be used here. Our earliest evidence so far is from 2021 in the context of the COVID pandemic where it was used as a derogatory term for people protesting the vaccine mandates and lockdowns. It has since grown to include people protesting a range of issues and as you say can be synonymous with ‘conspiracy theorist.’ It’s a relatively recent term so we’re still monitoring it but it has certainly found its way into popular discourse including parliamentary debate. The satirical website, the Betoota Advocate, posted two stories about bird vaccinations. The first clearly targeted the cookers: Cartoonist Pat Hudson shared his take on Instagram: As the story unfolded, the South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, declared a “significant escalation” in H5 bird flu in the state after the detection of three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns: Malinauskas said the cause of the deaths was presumed to be H5 bird flu. State authorities were also investigating a suspected case in a little penguin found on Kangaroo Island, with the premier telling the state parliament the development was ‘of particular concern.’ Separately, the Tasmanian government said it was investigating 28 little penguin deaths on King Island with testing under way to determine whether the birds died of H5 bird flu. In another development, officials detected bird flu in a seal in South Australia. It is the first confirmed case of the H5N1 virus found in mammals down under. So far, 1,000 penguins have been vaccinated. Fortunately, there have been no confirmed infections in domestic animals such as poultry. — Previously Published on globalvoices.org with Creative Commons License Join The Good Men Project as a Premium Member today. news.content: Skip to content Search this Site Search Texas A&M Stories Close Search Search All Stories Explore Topics Press Center Menu & Search View All Stories Share this Agriculture Researchers test new tool to fight bird flu in poultry Multiyear study aims to reduce pathogens in commercial chicken houses without harming birds. Sep. 4, 2026 By Karn Dhingra, Texas A&M AgriLife 4 min. read Researchers in the Texas A&M Department of Poultry Science are testing far-UVC light to determine whether it can reduce airborne pathogens in commercial poultry houses without harming birds. Credit: Michael Miller/Texas A&M AgriLife When a strain of highly pathogenic avian influenza, HPAI, tore through U.S. poultry farms in early 2025, farmers culled tens of millions of birds, and egg prices soared. The losses highlighted the poultry industry’s urgent need for additional tools and methods to limit the virus’ spread. Now, researchers from the Texas A&M College of Agriculture and Life Sciences are preparing to test a new potential line of defense. They will use a form of ultraviolet light called far-UVC to see if it can kill HPAI without harming birds on poultry farms. “The current HPAI outbreak began around 2022 and hasn’t ended,” said Morgan Farnell, avian microbiology and immunology professor, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service program leader and associate department head in the Texas A&M Department of Poultry Science. “Avian influenza is still being found in Texas wildlife. It is not considered to be endemic in the U.S. and is classified as a reportable poultry disease.” Farnell and Ziteng “Tim” Xu, Texas A&M AgriLife Research smart technologies in poultry production scientist and assistant professor in the Department of Poultry Science, will lead the third and final phase of a multiyear study starting in February, examining whether far-UVC light can reduce airborne pathogen loads inside commercial poultry houses. Testing far-UVC light in real-world conditions Far-UVC light differs from conventional germicidal UV light because it can inactivate viruses and bacteria without penetrating deeply enough to damage human or animal skin and eyes. Far-UVC light is of interest as an anti-pathogen tool because it could be used safely in occupied spaces such as hospitals, clinics, classrooms, restaurants and poultry houses. Researchers from Columbia University Center for Radiological Research and St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital are studying how effective far-UVC light is against pathogens in a specialized isolator. The results established the groundwork for further testing in commercial farm settings, Farnell said. Texas A&M’s role is to determine whether far-UVC performs similarly under commercial conditions. “The isolators used at St. Jude are small and not very representative of the real world,” Farnell said. “We’ll stock birds at commercial density and test it at Texas A&M.” Researchers will use air-sampling equipment to measure indicator organisms, including aerobic bacteria, coliforms and Staphylococcus aureus, before and after far-UVC exposure. Those readings will inform far-UVC’s potential impact on pathogens like HPAI. The Barbara J. Huffman and William M. “Bill” Huffman ’53 Poultry Science Farm Complex, where the trials will be conducted, along with the department’s Biosafety Level 2 laboratory and biosecurity and environmental sampling experience, made the university a natural partner for the project’s applied phase, Farnell said. Measuring how far-UVC works around birds Xu will focus on the engineering challenges of deploying the technology in poultry houses. Dust can absorb or scatter far-UVC light before it reaches spaces occupied by birds. His team will measure how much ultraviolet radiation reaches those areas. Using artificial intelligence-assisted camera tracking, researchers also will monitor whether the light will affect the behavior, circadian rhythms and growth performance in the chickens. Xu is also designing an integrated disinfection system that combines far-UVC air treatment with UVC-enabled positive-pressure ventilation and robotic floor-disinfection modules. The team will test which components are necessary to effectively control pathogens. If the project is successful, researchers could eventually apply the technology beyond poultry facilities to swine and dairy operations, Xu said. A potential new tool for poultry producers The study by Farnell and Xu will span two years and include four flocks, two raised under summer conditions and two under winter conditions. Farnell said the poultry industry needs new tools to protect bird health. The industry has steered away from using antibiotics over the past decade. However, vaccinating for avian influenza is problematic with broilers for a number of reasons. Any tool must maintain flock productivity to make economic sense for farmers, he said. Fewer infections could reduce mortality and economic losses throughout the poultry supply chain. “Anything to improve bird health improves animal welfare and ultimately creates better outcomes for producers,” Farnell said. The project is funded through a $2 million U.S. Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service grant from the Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Poultry Innovation Grand Challenge award

Sections Contact Newsletter Search Donate now Current language: English ThursdaySeptember 10, 2026 Central Asia Central Asia Caucasus Caucasus North Asia North Asia East Asia East Asia South East Asia South East Asia South Asia South Asia Middle East Middle East Oceania Oceania Vaticano Vaticano Homepage > East Asia > China More bird flu deaths in China and Indonesia Questions are raised after latest death is confirmed in area without any reported outbreak. Bird flu should reach the Americas within six-twelve months, says UN official. China - Indonesia - Russia - Hong Kong March 10, 2006 Beijing (AsiaNews/SCMP) A three-year-old Indonesian boy and a nine-year-old Chinese girl are the latest victims of the bird flu. In mainland China, Guangdong authorities want restrictions on poultry exports to Hong Kong lifted. Indonesia. The boy died on February 28 at the Samarang hospital in Central Java but World Health Organisation (WHO) official Hariadi Wibisono confirmed the news only today. His death brings the total toll to 21, but according to Wibisono several cases have not been checked. China. The girl from Zhejiang province died in the evening of March 6. She fell ill after visiting relatives on a farm in Guangde County, Anhui province, where poultry was infected. There have been no official report about outbreaks in this province but it seems unlikely the girl could have been infected in Zhejiang, near Shanghai. So far in China there have been 15 known cases of human bird flu infections in nine provinces. "It's likely that the poultry may be infected but there may not be large or obvious deaths of poultry to alert officials to an outbreak in the area," said Aphaluck Bhatiasevi, a WHO spokeswoman in Beijing. "The epidemic situation is very severe. Right now is spring, when there is a high chance of bird flu outbreaks due to the frequent movement of migratory birds," China's Deputy Agriculture Minister Yin Chengjie said. "Given the flight patterns of wild birds that have been spreading avian influenza from Asia to Europe and Africa, birds infected with the H5N1 virus could reach the Americas within the next six to 12 months," David Nabarro, senior UN coordinator for avian and human influenza, said on March 8. Meanwhile, Guangdong's Agriculture Department announced that its poultry is safe from bird flu and has appealed to Hong Kong to lift its ban on chicken imports. Yu Yedong, head of the provincial department's Animal Health Inspection and Quarantine Administration, said inspections were being increased to ensure that chicken stocks replenished after the Lunar New Year were vaccinated. Only some local 300 farms are accredited for exporting chickens to Hong Kong. The Food and Agriculture Organisation's regional co-ordinator for bird flu in Beijing, Guo Fusheng, said he believed that Guangdong's vaccination programme was effective because there had been no H5N1 outbreaks among birds. But there was still a risk that backyard chickens might not have been vaccinated and might end up in wet markets. "Guangdong has many backyard farms, especially in the northern and western parts of the province, and Cantonese people love to eat chicken from small farms," he said. Russia. An outbreak in poultry farm was confirmed in the southern region of Stavropol. Since the beginning of March more than 70,000 chickens have been culled.
